demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I force myself to think only positive thoughts
I try to push them out of my mind

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
I have to be on guard all the time
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination appraisals are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another person; for this trauma type, guilt, responsibility, danger, or moral failure would be more coherent than feeling physically dirty/contaminated, absent any assault or bodily violation context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: Other-blame rumination conflicts with the trauma type and the rest of the profile: the central event is that he accidentally injured another person, while the appraisals emphasize defectiveness and threat rather than victimization by others. Dwelling on what other people have done to me points to a different trauma narrative.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: Magical thinking that the event did not really happen or was not that bad sits awkwardly with the very high-severity profile and with simultaneous endorsement of full sensory reliving plus strong persistent threat and self-defectiveness. Partial minimization can occur, but this item as phrased is in notable tension with the rest of the profile.

vignette: At eighty, Devinder Kapoor lives in a quiet coastal neighborhood that still carries the salt-heavy air of his decades-long career with the Coast Guard. His symptoms began following a violent autumn gale on the outer bank, where a misjudged winch tension caused a deckhand to slip over the rail and sustain a severe spinal fracture. The accident fused landscape, sound, and language into a single threat matrix. Today, a walk through coastal marshland, the distant wail of a passing ambulance, or even a neighbor's casual remark about "what might happen down the road" instantly jolts his nervous system. Because these environmental cues pull disconnected fragments of the deck, the slick railing, and the heavy thud of boots forward before he can assemble them, they directly feed a full sensory reliving that feels completely real across all his senses at once. Stripped of the ability to deliberately recall the sequence when he tries to access it, the involuntary flood makes the present feel unbearably perilous, locking him into a state of relentless scanning where he must remain on guard at all times. The perceived immediacy of danger dictates his daily routing; he cannot step into unfamiliar neighborhoods where escape routes might be unknown, and in public spaces, he meticulously selects seats near exits or against solid walls, mapping every vantage point as if still on duty. The constant vigilance and the weight of the accident consolidate into a quiet, corrosive conviction: there is fundamentally something wrong with him as a person, that the tragedy occurred because of his inherent character. To survive this unbearable self-judgment, Devinder retreats into rigid mental controls. He tells himself the line didn't truly break or that the outcome wasn't as severe as his mind whispers. When that fails, he forces himself to focus exclusively on favorable outcomes, rehearsing cheerful stories to drown out the dark. He tries to push the images of the deckhand entirely out of his mind, treating memory like a storm surge he can dam with sheer will. Because he believes himself defective, these strategies become his only refuge; yet the more he suppresses the past, the more violently the fragmented pieces surface, ensuring the memory returns with greater intensity. The forced optimism curdles into shame, confirming his defective self-appraisal and ensuring that negative judgments harden into habit. His magical bargaining-swearing he'll never wear that old uniform again, or that if he just stays perfectly still, the past won't follow-actually heightens his alertness to environmental cues, meaning the very strategies meant to calm him amplify his triggers. In a desperate bid to reclaim agency against this deepening threat, he sometimes engages in reckless maneuvers, like pushing through severe weather to prove he can handle exposure, which only deepens the cycle of perceived danger. Over decades, these habits calcified into a self-reinforcing current: the avoidance of unknown spaces and the constant searching for a protected seat leave him isolated, while the risky stunts and mental silences ensure the accident is never truly processed, only postponed. What finally brought him to a clinic was a recent evening when a friend's offhand comment about "the next twenty years" triggered a full sensory flashback so intense he collapsed against his kitchen counter, convinced he was still failing to save a man. He seeks help not because he wants to relive the storm, but because he fears the loop will ultimately cost him his remaining decades in paralysis. He hopes, quietly, that someone might help him anchor the past without letting it drag him under, that he might finally be allowed to stop bracing for the line to snap.
